exercises.label: Exercise 10.B1 — Medium: Reserve space for a noisier sensor
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The current paragraph has the right numerical answer but jumps from sensor subtraction to the command bound. Explain the disturbance integral, why the affine lower bound controls the entire hold, actuator intersection, nearest-point selection, correction and explicit terminal arithmetic.
exercises.replacement_html:
Convert the noisier reading into a guaranteed current clearance. Let $d(0)$ be the true clearance in metres. The reading is $y=0.35$ and $|y-d(0)|\le0.08$, so $d(0)\ge y-0.08=0.27$. Write this lower bound as $d_{\min}=0.27$. The disturbance bound is still $|w(t)|\le0.1$ metres per second, and the command is held for $\Delta=0.5$ seconds.

Derive the condition for the whole holding interval. Integrating $\dot d=u+w(t)$ and using $w(t)\ge-0.1$ gives

$$d(t)=d(0)+ut+\int_0^t w(s)\,ds \ge0.27+(u-0.1)t,\qquad 0\le t\le0.5.$$

This lower bound is affine in time. Its minimum is at the beginning if $u-0.1\ge0$, and at the end if $u-0.1\lt0$. The beginning is already safe because $0.27\gt0$, so the terminal condition suffices in either case:

$$\begin{aligned} 0.27+0.5(u-0.1)&\ge0\\ 0.27+0.5u-0.05&\ge0\\ 0.5u&\ge-0.22\\ u&\ge-0.44. \end{aligned}$$

Choose the nearest available safe command. Intersecting this inequality with the actuator interval $[-0.8,0.8]$ gives $[-0.44,0.8]$ metres per second. The nominal request $u_{\rm nom}=-0.8$ is below every point in that interval, so its nearest feasible point is the lower endpoint, $u^\star=-0.44$. The signed correction is $u^\star-u_{\rm nom}=-0.44-(-0.8)=0.36$ metres per second: the robot approaches the boundary more slowly.

Check the limiting trajectory. At the smallest permitted current clearance and constant worst disturbance $w=-0.1$,

$$d(0.5)=0.27+0.5(-0.44-0.1) =0.27-0.27=0.$$

The worst trajectory reaches the boundary at the end and stays nonnegative before it; there is zero reserve left. Reusing the old command $-0.5$ would instead give $0.27+0.5(-0.5-0.1)=0.27-0.30=-0.03$ metres. Thus the old command fails under an allowed realization of the larger measurement error. This conclusion uses the stated immediate-velocity model and disturbance bounds for this hold; future holds require fresh valid measurements and feasible commands.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.B2 — Hard: A safe set can demand an unavailable actuator
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The feasibility answer and missing-control-direction conclusion are correct, but a beginning student needs the actual interval intersection, inequality rearrangement, equality endpoint and a trajectory showing why any positive hold fails at zero clearance. Separate temporary help from faster sampling at positive clearance from the impossibility of indefinite robustness.
exercises.replacement_html:
Find when safety and the damaged actuator can agree. Let $d_{\min}$ be the guaranteed nonnegative current clearance. For a half-second held command, the worst disturbance is $w=-0.1$, so the safety condition is

$$d_{\min}+0.5(u-0.1)\ge0 \iff u\ge0.1-2d_{\min}.$$

The damaged actuator permits only $-0.8\le u\le0$. Therefore its robust feasible set is

$$\left[\max\{-0.8,\,0.1-2d_{\min}\},\,0\right]$$

provided that the left endpoint is no greater than zero. Since $-0.8\le0$ already, this occurs precisely when

$$0.1-2d_{\min}\le0 \iff 0.1\le2d_{\min} \iff d_{\min}\ge0.05\ \text{metres}.$$

The smallest clearance is thus $0.05$ metres. At equality, the safety bound is $u\ge0$ and the actuator bound is $u\le0$, so the only feasible command is $u=0$. Its worst terminal clearance is $0.05+0.5(0-0.1)=0$.

Examine the boundary rather than extrapolating from a successful hold. At $d_{\min}=0$, the half-second condition becomes $u\ge0.1$, which the actuator cannot supply. More generally, for any hold length $\Delta\gt0$, the condition $0+\Delta(u-0.1)\ge0$ still requires $u\ge0.1$. An allowed initial state is $d(0)=0$. With the allowed disturbance $w=-0.1$ and every available $u\le0$, the actual derivative obeys $\dot d=u-0.1\le-0.1$, so $d(t)\le-0.1t\lt0$ for every $t\gt0$. Sampling faster does not change that missing outward velocity.

For a positive clearance, shortening a single hold can temporarily help: its condition is $d_{\min}\ge0.1\Delta$ when using the best available command $u=0$. It cannot provide indefinite robustness, however. Under the constant worst disturbance, even time-varying commands restricted to $u(t)\le0$ satisfy $d(t)\le d(0)-0.1t$, so every finite initial reserve is eventually exhausted. Continued robust operation needs a different physical backup capability or disturbance assumption. A finite-horizon operation may instead stop before exhausting its reserve; that is a different requirement from invariance for all time.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.B3 — Hard: Add the age of a measurement to its error budget
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The numerical values 0.14, -0.32 and -0.09 are right but the answer omits the triangle inequality connecting an old reading to the present state, the held-input derivation and actuator projection. Spell out these steps and keep the caveat about the past speed bound.
exercises.replacement_html:
Bring the old measurement forward to the present. Denote the measurement time by $t_s$ and the present time by $t_s+0.1$ seconds. At $t_s$, $|d(t_s)-y|\le0.05$ metres. The given speed bound holds throughout the delay, so

$$|d(t_s+0.1)-d(t_s)| \le\int_{t_s}^{t_s+0.1}|\dot d(s)|\,ds \le0.9(0.1)=0.09\ \text{metres}.$$

The triangle inequality adds the possible motion error to the original sensor error:

$$|d(t_s+0.1)-y| \le0.09+0.05=0.14\ \text{metres}.$$

Thus a valid present error bound is $0.14$ metres, and the guaranteed present clearance is $d_{\min}=0.35-0.14=0.21$ metres. The motion contribution can have the same unfavorable sign as the sensor error, so subtracting one uncertainty from the other would not be valid.

Recompute the safe held command from the present lower bound. During the next half-second the worst disturbance is again $-0.1$ metres per second. The affine lower bound is $d(t)\ge0.21+(u-0.1)t$ for $0\le t\le0.5$, with time now measured from the present. Its initial value is positive, so require its terminal value to be nonnegative:

$$\begin{aligned} 0.21+0.5(u-0.1)&\ge0\\ 0.5u&\ge0.05-0.21=-0.16\\ u&\ge-0.32. \end{aligned}$$

Intersecting with $[-0.8,0.8]$ gives $[-0.32,0.8]$. The request $-0.8$ is below the feasible interval, so the nearest command is $u^\star=-0.32$ metres per second. Its correction is $-0.32-(-0.8)=0.48$ metres per second. The selected worst terminal clearance is $0.21+0.5(-0.32-0.1)=0.21-0.21=0$.

Audit the proposed reuse. Holding the old command $-0.5$ instead gives

$$d_{\rm lower}(0.5)=0.21+0.5(-0.5-0.1) =0.21-0.30=-0.09\ \text{metres}.$$

With the smallest permitted present clearance and constant worst disturbance, the boundary is reached after $0.21/0.6=0.35$ seconds, before the half-second update. The old command is therefore unsafe under an allowed realization. The age correction relies on a valid speed bound during the entire past delay; the newly arrived reading cannot retroactively establish that assumption. Future safety also relies on the stated held-input model and timely updates.

pedagogical_review_basis: Actual method, notation/assumptions, intermediate reasoning, requested cases and result interpretation; no length metric.
